findings.finding: Insights: Scores become 20‑bit binary codes; round i sets the i‑th bit for each pair in equal‑score groups. Faster always wins, so the final ordering equals the speed order, but any pairing respecting scores is allowed. Count distinct final rankings = number of possible binary‑tree labelings consistent with total order. Compute N, find highest power of 10 dividing N, then k mod 10⁵. (Key: N = product of odd factorials; avoid overcounting identical scores.)

Insights: Winners/losers split each equal‑size group each round → a full binary tree of depth 20 where each node size = 2^{20‑i}. Any binary tree labeling of 2^{20} distinct speeds is realizable, giving all 2^{20}! orderings. N= (2^{20})!; k = ν₁₀(N); answer = k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Pairing by equal scores forces a perfect binary‑tree tournament; each runner’s final score is a unique 20‑bit binary number (wins = 1). Thus final rankings correspond exactly to the total order of the 2²⁰ distinct binary numbers, i.e. all 2²⁰! permutations. So N = (2²⁰)!. Find the largest k with 10^k | N → k = v₂(N)+v₅(N). Compute v₂((2²⁰)!) and v₅((2²⁰)!) via Legendre; k = Σ⌊2²⁰/2^i⌋ + Σ⌊2²⁰/5^i⌋. Then output k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Final scores are unique 0…2²⁰‑1, forming a binary tree of depth 20. Any runner can end at any leaf, but pairings restrict which permutations are realizable. N = #bijections of 2²⁰ runners onto leaves achievable via matchings. Compute v₂(N), v₅(N); k = min(v₂,v₅). Beware overcounting: pairings within each equal‑score group are independent; total count = product over rounds of (number of perfect matchings)^{#groups}. Use factorials: round i has 2^{20‑i} groups of size 2^{i}; each contributes (2^{i}‑1)!! matchings. Thus N = ∏_{i=1}^{20} ((2^{i}‑1)!! )^{2^{20‑i}}. Then v₂, v₅ from factorial exponents; k = min(v₂,v₅) mod 10⁵.

Insights: Final scores are unique 20‑bit numbers; each round i splits each equal‑score group into winners (bit 1) and losers (bit 0). Pairings are arbitrary matchings within groups, but faster always wins. A set of winners of size 2^{19} is realizable iff it can be matched to distinct slower losers → must be the 2^{19} fastest runners. Inductively, at every round each “1” subgroup must consist of the fastest half of its parent group. Thus the final ordering is forced: the binary‑tree of splits must always send the faster half left. Hence only one ordering possible → N=1, k=0, answer 0.

Insights: After each round, each score class halves; after 20 rounds each binary score 0…2²⁰‑1 appears exactly once. Any runner can get any score iff we can pair within each class so faster wins. Pair sorted runners adjacently → always possible. Thus any bijection between speeds and binary numbers is realizable. Hence N = (2²⁰)! . Find largest k with 10ᵏ | (2²⁰)!. Compute v₂ and v₅ of factorial; k = min(v₂,v₅). v₅ = Σ⌊2²⁰/5ⁱ⌋ = 2⁰⁰? compute. Then answer = k mod 10⁵. (All steps concise).

Insights: Final scores are distinct binary numbers (wins per round). Any ordering corresponds to a binary‑tree “heap” where each node’s winner beats its sibling. Count = number of linear extensions of a complete binary tournament poset = product_{i=0}^{19} (2^{i}!) . Compute v₂, v₅ of N; k = min(v₂,v₅) mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: assume all permutations possible; must use heap‑order extensions, not arbitrary.

Insights: After i rounds each runner’s score is a 20‑bit binary number (wins = 1). Pairings are any perfect matchings within equal‑score groups; faster always wins. Thus the tournament’s outcome equals all possible ways to assign each runner a binary win‑loss pattern consistent with “if A beats B then A’s pattern ≥ B’s lexicographically”. Compute N = #linear extensions of the poset of 2²⁰ binary strings ordered by bitwise dominance. Find k = v₁₀(N) and output k mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: ignore tie‑break permutations (they’re already counted by extensions); ensure the dominance order, not just total scores.

Insights: Scores are binary (20 bits). Final ranking = permutation of runners to leaves of a full binary tree. At each node of size 2n, winners (left child) must be a “ballot” set → Catalanₙ possibilities.  
Thus  
\(N=\prod_{m=0}^{19} \big(C_{2^{m}}\big)^{2^{19-m}}\) where \(C_n\) is Catalan.  
Compute \(v_5(N)=\sum_{m=0}^{19}2^{19-m}·v_5(C_{2^{m}})=121 818\).  
\(v_2(N)=524 287>v_5\), so \(k=v_5=121 818\).  
Answer: \(k\bmod10^5=21 818\).  

Pitfalls: assume each node independent; need ballot condition (Catalan), not any split. Verify with small cases.

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit strings; ranking = lexicographic order of these strings. At each round (node of size 2^k) we must pick exactly half the runners as “winners” (bit 1) such that in the speed order, every prefix has ≥ ½ winners. This is the ballot condition, counted by Catalan C_{2^{k‑1}}. The tournament’s choices are independent across nodes, so total orderings N = ∏_{k=1}^{20} C_{2^{k‑1}}. Compute N’s 10‑adic valuation k = Σ_{k=1}^{20} ν_{10}(C_{2^{k‑1}}). Then answer = k mod 10^5. Pitfalls: ensure Catalan formula C_n = (2n choose n)/(n+1); use Legendre’s formula for ν_p of factorials; handle large n (up to 2^{19}) via prime‑wise sums.

Insights: Winners/losers at each node (size 2n) must satisfy “#wins≤#losses” in every speed‑prefix → Catalan Cₙ possibilities. Nodes are independent.  

N = ∏_{t=1}^{20} C_{2^{t-1}}^{2^{20‑t}}.  

v₂(C_{2^m})=1 (m≥1), v₅(C_{2^m}) computed via v₅((2n)!)-2v₅(n!)-v₅(n+1).  

Values v₅(C_{2^m}) for m=0…19: 0,0,0,1,1,0,2,1,0,1,1,3,3,4,0,2,3,5,4,6.  

v₅(N)=Σ_{m=0}^{19}2^{19‑m}·v₅(C_{2^m})=121 818.  

k = min(v₂(N),v₅(N)) = 121 818.  

k mod 10⁵ = **21818**.  

Pitfalls: assume any winner set works → need Dyck condition; compute v₅ correctly (include n+1 factor).

Insights: After 20 rounds each runner gets a unique 20‑bit win‑loss code → distinct scores 0…2²⁰‑1. Pairings force every pair to meet at the first differing bit; the faster must have 1 there. Thus the speed order must be a linear extension of the “binary‑tree” poset where for any node all left‑subtree elements outrank right‑subtree ones. Count linear extensions of this poset (size 2²⁰). Compute exponent k of 10 dividing that count; answer = k mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: assuming total order; must use Hall’s condition for feasible winner sets; recursion for extensions isn’t simply squaring. Use DP on tree: L(node)=C(Lsize_left+Lsize_right, Lsize_left)·L(left)·L(right). Compute 10‑adic valuation via Legendre’s formula.

Insights: After each round, winners (bit 1) precede losers (bit 0); groups split independently. First‑round winner set of size 2^{m‑1} must admit a perfect matching where each winner beats a slower loser → Dyck condition → Catalan C_{2^{m‑1}} possibilities.
